strengths: Clear problem identification and value as a benchmark: The computer vision fall detection literature has long suffered from fragmented, small-scale, and artificially staged datasets with incompatible annotations. Unifying eight public datasets under a standardized ten-class taxonomy (spanning transient actions and sustained states like 'fallen') provides a much-needed standardized testbed.

Introduction of the staged-to-wild evaluation protocol (OOPS-Fall): Testing models trained on controlled, staged laboratory settings against genuine in-the-wild accident videos from OOPS! explicitly exposes the significant generalization gap and domain shift in automated fall detection.

Systematic protocol design and domain analysis: The inclusion of rigorous cross-subject and cross-view splits, along with pairwise Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) and manifold visualizations (t-SNE, H-NNE), provides useful diagnostic insights into why feature representations (e.g., I3D vs. VideoMAE) generalize differently across domains.
weaknesses: Ecological validity of OOPS-Fall for target clinical populations: While OOPS! contains genuine accident footage, it primarily comprises user-uploaded viral or comedic accidents involving younger subjects, diverse camera motions, and novel outdoor activities. This domain does not closely represent genuine geriatric falls occurring in indoor eldercare or home-monitoring environments.

Limited exploration of modern architectures and adaptation methods: The technical experimentation is confined to frozen features from standard backbones (I3D and VideoMAE) with a lightweight classification head and MS-TCN++. The paper would be substantially stronger if it evaluated end-to-end fine-tuning, domain adaptation baselines, or modern video-language/multimodal foundation models.

Scope and scale of the unified dataset: Despite aggregating eight datasets, the total single-view duration remains around 14 hours across only 101 subjects, reflecting the overall scarcity of video fall data and limiting the complexity of models that can be trained from scratch without heavy pre-training priors.

strengths: Addresses a well-known bottleneck in video-based fall detection: the reliance on isolated, visually homogeneous, staged datasets with disparate annotation schemes and lack of realistic out-of-distribution evaluation.

Careful formulation and re-annotation of 8 public datasets into a unified 10-class taxonomy that explicitly distinguishes dynamic transition actions (fall, sit down, lie down, stand up) from static postures (fallen, sitting, lying, standing), which is of high clinical relevance for detecting 'long-lie' scenarios.
Introduction of the OOPS-Fall test set to establish an out-of-distribution staged-to-wild evaluation protocol, offering realistic insights into model transferability.

Interesting and insightful empirical analysis comparing frozen feature backbones (I3D vs. VideoMAE variants), highlighting that while transformer models fit controlled benchmarks better, simpler motion-oriented representations (I3D) generalize significantly better to in-the-wild falls.
weaknesses: The benchmark relies on re-annotating existing public datasets and curating internet accident clips from OOPS; it does not introduce new primary recording data from target demographics (e.g., geriatric populations in clinical or home care settings). As noted in the limitations, web accidents differ notably from elderly fall mechanics.

The baseline evaluation is limited to frozen feature extractors coupled with lightweight temporal classifiers and MS-TCN++; exploring end-to-end fine-tuning, temporal action detection architectures, or domain adaptation methods would make the benchmark analysis more thorough.

Code:') with missing URLs, and references to tables in the supplementary material (e.g., VMAE-K400-Pre) leave some statements in Section 4.2 without immediate in-text table backing.

strengths: High-impact application and strong motivation: Automated fall detection and long-lie detection are crucial for elder care, yet the field has suffered from fragmented, non-standardized, and visually homogenous staged datasets.

Comprehensive benchmark unification: The paper systematically gathers 8 public datasets following PRISMA guidelines, standardizes them under a coherent 10-class taxonomy separating transient movements (e.g., fall, lie down) from persistent postures (e.g., fallen, lying), and provides clean cross-subject and cross-view splits.

Staged-to-wild evaluation (OOPS-Fall): Introducing a curated set of authentic accidents from uncontrolled video (OOPS!) establishes a much-needed benchmark protocol for measuring out-of-distribution generalization to real-world accidents.

Insightful empirical findings: The experiments provide valuable insights, notably revealing that frozen convolutional representations (I3D) generalize significantly better to out-of-distribution real falls than self-supervised visual transformers (VideoMAE), which tend to overfit the controlled environment appearance.
weaknesses: Reliance strictly on frozen backbones: Experiments exclusively evaluate frozen feature extractors coupled with lightweight temporal classifiers or MS-TCN++. It remains unclear whether end-to-end fine-tuning, adapter-based tuning, or prompt-tuning on modern video foundation models could mitigate the observed out-of-distribution performance drops.

Demographic mismatch in the in-the-wild dataset: OOPS-Fall is derived from internet fail/accident videos featuring mostly young, agile individuals engaged in diverse activities. While uncontrolled visually, the fall mechanics, speeds, and context diverge noticeably from geriatric falls in assisted living or domestic elder care.

Absence of pose-based or multimodal baselines: Several constituent datasets (e.g., CMDFall, UP Fall) provide depth, inertial, or 3D data, and standard fall detection literature heavily utilizes 2D/3D human pose estimators to bypass background domain shifts. Including a pose-based action recognition baseline would significantly strengthen the benchmark comparison.
Minor presentation omissions: Under the abstract on page 1, there are blank placeholder lines ('OmniFall:' and 'Code:') where project URLs or repository placeholders were left incomplete.

strengths: Substantial benchmark curation and standardization effort: The paper harmonizes eight disparate public staged fall detection datasets under a unified 16-class taxonomy with standardized cross-subject and cross-view splits, providing dense frame-level annotations for both classification and temporal action segmentation.

First standardized 'In-the-Wild' test benchmark: By curating and densely annotating 818 genuine accident clips from the OOPS dataset, the benchmark establishes a realistic, out-of-distribution evaluation bed to diagnose whether models trained in staged lab setups generalize to real-world falls.

Well-structured synthetic dataset with demographic control: OF-Synthetic generates 12,000 clips using Wan 2.2 with systematic factorial variation over demographic attributes (age groups, Monk skin tones, BMI bands) and camera viewpoints, offering a privacy-preserving training corpus and enabling cross-attribute fairness/bias evaluations.

Valuable empirical findings: Experiments reveal critical insights for the community—specifically, that synthetic video data can match or surpass real staged data for out-of-distribution transfer to wild accidents (64.2% vs. 60.5-61.2% Fall F1), and that appearance representations (SigLIP2) and motion representations (I3D) exhibit distinct sensitivities across synthetic and staged regimes.

Comprehensive documentation and protocol clarity: The appendix provides transparent documentation, including systematic dataset search adhering to PRISMA guidelines, explicit licensing details, prompt templates, and reproducible split definitions.
weaknesses: Domain disparity between 'OOPS' fails and target clinical/elderly falls: While OF-In-the-Wild provides authentic camera motion and uncontrolled environments, sourcing clips primarily from the OOPS dataset means the falls are largely viral accidental fails (often younger individuals, sports, or outdoor stunts) rather than typical frail elderly falls or syncopal episodes in residential/care facilities.

Temporal and physical limitations of diffusion-generated videos: The 12k synthetic videos average ~5 seconds per clip with relatively low temporal complexity. Video diffusion models frequently struggle with realistic physical dynamics, impact velocities, and biomechanical realism during rapid loss-of-balance events compared to physics-based simulations or real footage.

Minor inconsistency in classification implementation description: Section 4.2 states that VideoMAE-K400 is fine-tuned 'end-to-end' on the benchmark datasets, whereas Section A.5 (Implementation details action classification) describes training a lightweight temporal transformer over frozen pre-extracted features. Clarifying whether the backbone was fully fine-tuned or probed linearly/temporally is important for reproducibility.

Absence of novel algorithmic solutions: The paper serves purely as a dataset and benchmark contribution relying on standard baseline models (VideoMAE, ASQuery, TW-FINCH). While baseline benchmarking is appropriate for a Datasets/Benchmarks track, proposing a baseline domain adaptation or pre-training strategy tailored to the identified synthetic-to-wild gap would have strengthened the technical contribution.

strengths: Compelling problem formulation addressing critical flaws in vision-based fall detection: lack of standardized protocols, small and homogeneous staged datasets, ethical hurdles in acquiring elderly fall data, and absence of standardized real accident evaluation.

Substantial benchmark curation and annotation effort: harmonizing eight public staged datasets under a unified 16-class framewise taxonomy (distinguishing transient actions like 'fall' from persistent states like 'fallen' and non-critical actions like 'lying down'), paired with a curated real accident test set (OF-ItW) and 12,000 synthetic videos (OF-Syn).

Principled demographic and visual factor control in synthetic video generation: leveraging the Wan 2.2 diffusion model with explicit control over age brackets, OMB racial categories, Monk skin tones, BMI bands, and camera configurations, enabling controlled cross-demographic evaluation.

Insightful experimental findings on sim-to-real and cross-domain transfer: showing that demographic and visual diversity in synthetic data allows it to match or exceed real staged data when generalizing to in-the-wild accidents, with complementary behavior across appearance-centric (SigLIP2) and motion-centric (I3D) representations.
Thorough supplementary documentation, including systematic PRISMA review protocol, detailed cross-subject/cross-view splits, VIA annotation pipelines, and qualitative domain shift visualizations.
weaknesses: Nature of the 'in-the-wild' target distribution: OF-ItW is sourced from the OOPS! unintentional action dataset, which predominantly contains internet fail videos (viral slips, outdoor sports/play mishaps, active younger individuals). This distribution differs notably from typical clinical or elderly domestic falls (indoor, frailty-driven, slow descents), which may limit the clinical transferability of conclusions drawn from OF-ItW.

Potential scene/context confound in synthetic vs. staged comparison: The paper notes that both OF-Syn and OF-ItW contain numerous outdoor activities, whereas all staged datasets are strictly indoors. It is unclear whether OF-Syn's advantage over OF-Staged on OF-ItW is driven by superior fall dynamics/demographics or simply shared scene context (indoor vs. outdoor background diversity). An evaluation on indoor-only wild clips would clarify this.
Minor editorial issues and typos in the manuscript (e.g., in Section 4.2: 'correlateAll our dataset contributions', repeated words 'training. training.', and crowded radar plot labels in Figure 6).

strengths: Substantial and impactful benchmark contribution: OmniFall addresses long-standing fragmentation and staging bias in vision-based fall detection by harmonizing 8 staged datasets (OF-Staged), curating a genuine accident test set (OF-ItW), and generating a systematically controlled synthetic dataset (OF-Syn).

Dense, frame-level annotation across a coherent 16-class taxonomy that explicitly distinguishes transient dynamic transitions (fall, sit down, lie down) from persistent static states (fallen, lying, sitting), which is medically crucial for resolving the 'long-lie' problem in real-world care monitoring.

Rigorously designed data curation and standardized protocols: systematic PRISMA literature review for staged dataset inclusion, explicit cross-subject and cross-view splits, and controlled prompt templates across demographic axes (age, Monk skin tone, BMI bands).

Compelling empirical insights: demonstrates that diverse synthetic video training can match or outperform staged real video datasets on wild transfer (Fall F1 of 64.2% vs 60.5-61.2%), and provides nuanced analysis showing appearance-based features (SigLIP2) transfer better from synthetic data while motion-based features (I3D) rely more on real staged dynamics.
weaknesses: Limited backbone diversity in the classification experiments: only VideoMAE-K400 is fine-tuned for end-to-end classification across the benchmark datasets; testing additional temporal/video backbones or video-LLMs would verify whether the synthetic-to-wild transfer advantages generalize across model families.

Domain mismatch between viral accidents and clinical elderly falls: OF-In-the-Wild is derived from the OOPS dataset, which primarily captures internet fail/accident videos (often active/younger adults in outdoors/sports). While valuable as an out-of-distribution wild test, it still differs meaningfully from typical geriatric indoor falls caused by frailty or medical events.

Potential physical inaccuracies in diffusion-generated motions: synthetic videos produced via text-to-video models (Wan 2.2) can exhibit unrealistic impact physics, morphing, or temporal discontinuities during sudden drops, which may explain why motion-centric representations (I3D) struggle on synthetic training data.
Minor typographical errors in the manuscript, such as repeated phrases ('training. training.' on page 7) and typos in appendix figure captions ('ID3' instead of 'I3D' in Figures 9–12).
